content: When intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) was first introduced for newborns suffering from hypoxic respiratory failure due to hyaline membrane disease (HMD), mortality rates were alarmingly high, and air leaks were a significant complication. These air leaks, a form of barotrauma, were primarily caused by the high peak inspiratory pressures (PIP) required to oxygenate the stiff, non-compliant lungs of these infants. The key factors influencing mean airway pressure—and consequently oxygenation—on conventional ventilators include inspiratory time (IT), PIP, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP), and gas flow rates. In the 1970s, small, uncontrolled studies suggested that using a prolonged inspiratory time (IT) combined with slower ventilatory rates could reduce barotrauma. This approach was subsequently adopted widely. However, despite advancements in neonatal ventilator technology aimed at minimizing lung injury, the incidence of bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) remains persistently high. Therefore, it is critical to identify the inspiratory time that minimizes harm in mechanically ventilated neonates. The objective of this review was to determine whether a long inspiratory time, compared to a short inspiratory time, reduces the rates of death, air leaks, and BPD in mechanically ventilated newborns. To address this question, the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group (CNRG) conducted a systematic search of electronic databases, including MEDLINE (1966–April 2004) and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, Issue 4, 2003). Additionally, abstracts from the Society for Pediatric Research and the European Society for Pediatric Research (1998–2003) were reviewed to identify unpublished trials. The inclusion criteria encompassed all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving mechanically ventilated infants, with or without respiratory pathology, that compared long versus short IT. Randomized crossover studies focusing on oxygenation differences were also included. Data collection and analysis followed the standard methodology of the Cochrane Collaboration and its Neonatal Review Group. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and methodological quality of each trial and extracted data. The results were analyzed using relative risk (RR), risk difference (RD), and their 95% confidence intervals (CIs). A fixed-effect model was employed for meta-analyses. The review included five studies involving a total of 694 infants. The use of a long IT was associated with a statistically significant increase in the incidence of air leaks, with a typical relative risk (RR) of 1.56 (95% CI: 1.25–1.94), a risk difference (RD) of 0.13 (95% CI: 0.07–0.20), and a number needed to treat (NNT) of 8 (95% CI: 5–14). There was no significant difference in the incidence of BPD between the long and short IT groups. However, a long IT was associated with an increase in mortality before hospital discharge, which approached borderline statistical significance, with a typical RR of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.00–1.59) and an RD of 0.07 (95% CI: 0.00–0.13). The authors concluded that caution is warranted when applying these findings to modern neonatal intensive care practices. The studies included in this review were conducted before the widespread use of antenatal steroids, postnatal surfactant therapy, and synchronized ventilatory support modes. Furthermore, most of the infants in these studies had a single pathology (HMD), and no studies evaluated the effects of IT on newborns ventilated for other conditions, such as meconium aspiration syndrome or congenital heart disease, where lung compliance is normal. Nevertheless, the observed increase in air leaks and mortality associated with long ITs is clinically significant. Therefore, it is recommended that infants with poorly compliant lungs be ventilated using a short inspiratory time.
